nameStory: The cutlip minnow gets its distinctive name from its truly bizarre mouth structure. Unlike any other minnow, its lower jaw has three lobes, with the middle one protruding like a tiny tongue or 'cut lip' that's been split open. This strange adaptation makes it instantly recognizable among New England's minnow species.
description: The cutlip minnow is a medium-sized freshwater fish that averages about 6 inches long with an olive-green coloration. What makes this minnow absolutely unmistakable is its weird three-lobed lower jaw with a protruding middle section that looks like a little tongue sticking out. It's a stream-dwelling fish that prefers clear, rocky pools where it can use that specialized mouth to scrape tiny shellfish and other food from stones. While not flashy in appearance, its unique mouth structure sets it apart from every other minnow you'll encounter.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Three-lobed lower jaw with the middle lobe protruding like a pink tongue - absolutely unique among all New England minnows and unmistakable once you see it

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Typical minnow body shape, streamlined and torpedo-like, feels firm and muscular when handled, about as thick as your thumb

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Olive-green back fading to lighter sides, not particularly vibrant but with a healthy, natural sheen when fresh from the water

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized minnow averaging 6 inches - bigger than most small minnows but not huge, fits comfortably in your palm

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in clear, stony pools of streams rather than fast rapids - look for them hovering near rocky bottoms where they can scrape food

habitat: Cutlip minnows live in running streams throughout New England, showing a strong preference for clear water with stony bottoms. They avoid fast rapids, instead favoring the quieter pools where rocks provide plenty of surface area for the tiny shellfish and algae they scrape off with their specialized mouths. You'll find them in streams with good water quality and rocky substrates.

seasonality.spring: Late spring is spawning season when males build impressive stone nests up to 18 inches across - look for these circular rock formations in stream pools. Fish are most active and easiest to observe during this period.
seasonality.summer: Fish remain in their preferred rocky pools, actively feeding by scraping rocks with their distinctive mouths. This is when their olive-green coloration is most apparent.
seasonality.fall: Continue normal feeding behaviors in rocky stream pools. Fish may be slightly less active as water temperatures begin to cool.
seasonality.winter: Less active in colder water but still present in their rocky pool habitats. May be found in deeper pools where water temperatures remain more stable.

funFact: When food gets scarce or competition heats up, cutlip minnows turn into tiny aquatic pirates - they'll actually pluck out and eat the eyes of other fish, including their own species, as a protein-rich snack supplement!
confusionNotes: The cutlip minnow's three-lobed lower jaw makes it virtually impossible to confuse with any other fish species - no other minnow in New England has anything close to this bizarre mouth structure. If you see that protruding tongue-like middle lobe, you've found a cutlip minnow.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'minnow,' cutlip minnows are actually decent-sized fish that some anglers enjoy as panfish. The term 'minnow' here refers to the fish family rather than size - many minnows are actually quite substantial fish, not just tiny baitfish.
compareHints: The cutlip minnow is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our minnow species. Compared to other minnows in the same family like shiners and daces, the cutlip's three-lobed jaw is completely distinctive - no other minnow has developed this specialized rock-scraping mouth adaptation. While other minnows may be similar in size and general body shape, that bizarre lower jaw instantly sets the cutlip apart.
